messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mr. Sharma is a 50-year-old South Asian male who has been married for over two decades and works as an animator in Los Angeles. Mr. Sharma's life took a dramatic turn when his young daughter fell gravely ill, necessitating extensive medical treatment. The experience left him deeply traumatized, marked by specific triggers that now dominate his daily life. Mr. Sharma finds it almost impossible to sleep alone or in unfamiliar places. He has vivid flashbacks of the night when he discovered his daughter's illness and the frantic drive to the hospital under a starless sky. This trauma is further triggered whenever he smells antiseptic, reminiscent of the sterile environments where his daughter was treated for months. The mere thought of undergoing any medical procedure sends him into a state of heightened anxiety. The overwhelming triggers have led Mr. Sharma to adopt several maladaptive strategies in an attempt to cope with his PTSD symptoms. He often ruminates about how he could have prevented his daughter's illness or even seeks revenge on some abstract notion of the source, which only deepens his distress. In addition, he mentally rehearses worst-case scenarios repeatedly, believing that this preparation will somehow shield him from future trauma. These strategies provide a fleeting sense of control but ultimately exacerbate his anxiety. What frightens Mr. Sharma most is the fear of reliving those moments where he felt utterly helpless and vulnerable. The rumination and mental rehearsal of worst-case scenarios keep these traumatic memories vividly alive, making it nearly impossible for him to break free from their grip. He frequently asks others for reassurance that everything will be okay, a behavior that offers temporary relief but reinforces his underlying anxiety. Mr. Sharma’s occupation as an animator provides a backdrop where these triggers and maladaptive strategies often intersect. The sterile smell of the medical office where he had to undergo routine check-ups sends waves of panic through him. His sleep disturbances have affected his ability to concentrate at work, leading to missed deadlines and increased stress from projects piling up. The cycle that Mr. Sharma has fallen into is particularly distressing. When triggered by hospital smells or a medical examination, his anxiety spikes, prompting him to ruminate on past events and mentally rehearse worst-case scenarios. This maladaptive coping mechanism then heightens his vigilance for future triggers, creating a self-reinforcing loop of fear and avoidance. It was the compounded effect of these symptoms that finally pushed Mr. Sharma to seek help. He has become increasingly aware that his strategies are not working and that his relationships with both his wife and colleagues have been strained as a result. He is most afraid of losing control again, but he hopes for a way to regain some semblance of normalcy in his life. In his current state, Mr. Sharma struggles daily with the fear of reliving those traumatic moments. He is acutely aware that his coping mechanisms are only making things worse and is seeking help to break this cycle before it consumes him completely.
